note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — LONG LANCE-SHAPED SPIKELETS
tiles.details: Follow the actual Dave Richardson green panicle (panel 0) from its short branches into densely crowded lance-shaped, multi-flowered spikelets. Then examine Yves Bas's dried spikelets (panel 7) with fine outcurving awns and bract edge hairs. Four additional CC BY Texas-source photos now provide a live Austin green head (panel 8), dry attached flowering culm (panel 9), and Burnet green mature spikelet (panel 10); panel 11 gives lower sheaths near soil. None shows extracted roots, a real millimeter scale, or separated glume nerves. FNA gives spikelets about 20–50 mm with 7–20 florets; count and measure on a source-authenticated mature specimen.
tiles.short: Introduced annual; mature spikelets often 25–50 mm long with about 8–20 fertile florets.
tiles.status: SIX SOURCE-LABELLED REAL PHOTOS: TWO ORIGINAL + FOUR TEXAS FIELD/REPRODUCTIVE, ROOT CROWN STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · ANNUAL ROOTS, SHEATH AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: FNA reports an annual with soft white hairs often on the leaf sheaths and a 1–2-mm obtuse or erose true ligule. GrassBase describes an eciliate membrane, so verify the actual free edge rather than assuming its fringe. New Texas panel 11 shows a true lower flowering culm and leaf/sheath exterior above soil, with actual roots hidden, and DOES NOT expose a calibrated inner ligule. The older two target photos showed only heads; sheath hairs remain unverified at macro scale. A Texas specimen under synonym Bromus macrostachys (TEX-LL 00314236, Cliff Morden 21, 27 April 1980, Washington County) DOES picture dried fibrous roots and flowering stems, but scan reuse rights have not been confirmed: it is a RESEARCH-ONLY lead, not a public gallery photo. Obtain licensed same-plant rooted base, flowering axis and true 1-mm-scaled ligule.
tiles.short: Verify an annual fibrous-rooted plant and the approximately 1–2 mm true membranous ligule.
tiles.status: REAL LOWER SHOOT/SHEATH EXTERIOR PHOTOGRAPHED (PANEL 11); TRUE INNER LIGULE, ROOTED ANNUAL CROWN STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · BACKLIGHT THE TWO GLUMES
tiles.details: On ONE ripe target spikelet, separate both basal GLUMES and count their longitudinal veins by backlighting against a 1-mm ruler. FNA gives lower 3–5 and upper 5–7; Kew GrassBase generally gives lower 3 and upper 7–9. Those are published ranges, not measurements visible in panels 0, 7, or the newly archived Texas close green spikelet panel 10. For the native comparison, panel 3 is B. texensis, often 1-veined lower/3-veined upper; never mistake its photo for a laceolate brome organ.
tiles.short: Lower glume commonly 3–5-veined; upper reported about 5–9-veined across treatments.
tiles.status: TWO MEASURED BACKLIT GLUMES REQUIRED — TREATMENT VEIN RANGES DIFFER

tiles.heading: 04 · LEMMA BODY, TWO TIP TEETH AND AWN
tiles.details: Yves Bas's dry macro (panel 7) shows true species-labelled overlapping pointed bracts, twisted/slender awns and fine edge hairs, not an independently detached lemma. FNA describes fertile lemmas about 11–20 mm and awns mostly 6–12 mm, sometimes longer. The added Texas close green spikelet (panel 10) shows overlapping pointed bracts and outward awns but not their anatomical insertion. Confirm the two short tip teeth and SUBAPICAL awn insertion on a separated floret with physical 1-mm scale. Do not arrow a crowded awn tip as a precisely assigned lemma origin without a visible continuous connection.
tiles.short: Fertile lemma often 12–18 mm; awn approximately 6–12 mm, arising below the tip.
tiles.status: REAL BRACT PHOTO — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO DETACHED MEASURED LEMMA

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES — NATIVE FIRST
tiles.details: TARGET panels 0/7/8/9/10/11 are genuine B. lanceolatus, with four new CC BY Texas images. Panel 3 is NATIVE B. texensis, not panel 4. Panel 1 and panel 2 both point to the SAME Matt Lavin Japanese-brome JPEG, so they do not supply two independent comparison images. Panel 4 is native perennial hairy woodland brome B. pubescens; panels 5/6 are introduced broad-spikeleted rescuegrass B. catharticus. FNA lanceolate brome panicle branches are usually relatively rigid and shorter than the often 20–50-mm spikelets, as opposed to Japanese brome's often more flexuous panicle; appearances overlap, so confirm glumes and lemma before removal.
tiles.short: Native Texas brome = panel 3; Japanese brome duplicate = panels 1 and 2
tiles.status: SIX GENUINE TARGET PHOTOS + LABELED COMPARISON BROMES; COMPARATIVE GLUME/LEMMA DISSECTION NEEDED

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — TWO LANE HANDOFFS
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: real source-vouchered live annual rooted crown with attached flowering stem; hair distribution on lower sheaths; true membranous inner ligule 1–2 mm beside ruler; whole measured flowering head; two separated backlit glumes showing vein counts; mature isolated lemma and awn insertion, compared with B. texensis. NEEDS_SITE_QA: all six archived exact species photographs (four new Texas photos individually source-licensed), existing validated gross arrows, correction of the native Texas-brome comparison marker, duplicate Japanese comparison, mobile view and Pages build. Texas root-bearing herbarium voucher 00314236 is a rights-uncleared research lead ONLY. Four actual Texas species JPEGs installed in this pass; no new arrows, and no claims about microscopic glume or lemma anatomy.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — crown, ligule and glumes remain

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: INTRODUCED LANCEOLATE BROME: on the panicle find exceptionally LONG, narrow, pointed multi-flowered spikelets (typically ~25–50 mm) with EIGHT TO TWENTY florets. Measure spikelet body excluding awns; count florets and check lemma body ~12–18 mm under magnification. Do not mistake broad FLAT short-awn rescuegrass spikelets for the long narrowly tapering lanceolate form.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: 1 · GREEN TARGET: gallery 0, actual Dave Richardson panicle with green dense many-flowered spikelets; roots hidden.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: FNA reports an annual with soft white hairs often on the leaf sheaths and a 1–2-mm obtuse or erose true ligule. GrassBase describes an eciliate membrane, so verify the actual free edge rather than assuming its fringe. New Texas panel 11 shows a true lower flowering culm and leaf/sheath exterior above soil, with actual roots hidden, and DOES NOT expose a calibrated inner ligule. The older two target photos showed only heads; sheath hairs remain unverified at macro scale. A Texas specimen under synonym Bromus macrostachys (TEX-LL 00314236, Cliff Morden 21, 27 April 1980, Washington County) DOES picture dried fibrous roots and flowering stems, but scan reuse rights have not been confirmed: it is a RESEARCH-ONLY lead, not a public gallery photo. Obtain licensed same-plant rooted base, flowering axis and true 1-mm-scaled ligule.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Follow the actual Dave Richardson green panicle (panel 0) from its short branches into densely crowded lance-shaped, multi-flowered spikelets. Then examine Yves Bas's dried spikelets (panel 7) with fine outcurving awns and bract edge hairs. Four additional CC BY Texas-source photos now provide a live Austin green head (panel 8), dry attached flowering culm (panel 9), and Burnet green mature spikelet (panel 10); panel 11 gives lower sheaths near soil. None shows extracted roots, a real millimeter scale, or separated glume nerves. FNA gives spikelets about 20–50 mm with 7–20 florets; count and measure on a source-authenticated mature specimen.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Japanese brome — Bromus japonicus: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair. Lanceolate brome — Bromus lanceolatus: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle. Hairy woodland brome — Bromus pubescens: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma. Texas brome — Bromus texensis: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm. Rescuegrass — Bromus catharticus (comparison only): Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

memory_rule: JAPANESE: annual, flexuous awned head, higher glume veins. TEXAS: annual, lower ONE & upper THREE glume veins. LANCEOLATE: giant many-flowered spikelets. WOODLAND: perennial + hairy lemmas. RESCUE: broad flat short/no-awn units (comparison only).

field_rule: For native versus introduced Bromus, the important structures are glume VEINS, actual lemma dimensions and awns, and an annual or perennial rooted crown—not the word 'brome' or a pretty nodding head.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
